// shapes.ts.txt — SCANNED, NEVER RUN. The grammar allows callee shapes that a
// runnable .mjs cannot spell (TS non-null) or that only appear in positions
// the executable fixture has no use for. They are here so the CLASSIFIER is
// measured against the grammar, while the ORACLE is measured against what
// runs. The two denominators are different and saying so is the point.
//
// THE `.txt` TAIL IS LOAD-BEARING. tsconfig's include covers `test/**/*.ts`,
// so a fixture named `shapes.ts` is COMPILED as part of the project — and a
// fixture whose whole job is to hold odd or deliberately degenerate shapes
// cannot also satisfy tsc. The first version of this file was bent to please
// the compiler (`(0, curried)` grew a side effect to dodge TS2695), which
// silently changed the construct under study. The name keeps `.ts` so the
// reader and the scanner still know what language it is.
declare const maybe: ((n: number) => number) | null;
declare const bag: Record<string, (n: number) => number>;
declare const key: string;

export function tsShapes(n: number): number {
  return maybe!(n) + bag[key](n) + bag['fixed'](n);
}


class Base { m(): number { return 1; } }
export class Sub extends Base {
  constructor() { super(); }
  m(): number { return super.m(); }
}

// TWO SITES ADDED AS A MEASUREMENT, 2026-09-04. The grammar allows a member on
// a fresh instance and a member on an inline object literal; the corpus did
// not contain either, so whether the rules already cover them was a GUESS. A
// site turns the guess into a row. Neither needs a rule if `new C()` reaches
// the class and an object literal is its own value — and if it does need one,
// that is worth knowing before the cell is filled from an argument.
export function onNew(n: number): number { return new Base().m() + n; }
export function onLit(n: number): number { return ({ a(m: number) { return m; } }).a(n); }

function curried(n: number) { return (m: number) => m + n; }
export function chained(n: number): number { return curried(n)(n); }
export function seq(n: number): number { return (0, curried)(n)(n); }
export function cond(n: number, f: (x: number) => number, g: (x: number) => number) {
  return (n > 0 ? f : g)(n);
}
// TWO MORE MEASUREMENT SITES, 2026-09-04, and for the same reason as the last
// pair: `maybe!()` and `(c ? f : g)()` refused, and the refusal was about the
// CORPUS — `maybe` is an ambient declaration with no value, and nobody calls
// `cond`, so its parameters carry nothing. Give each a callee the value layer
// can actually reach and the question becomes about the model instead.
const notNull = curried;
export function useNonNull(n: number): number { return notNull!(n)(n); }
export function useCond(n: number): number { return cond(n, curried(1), curried(2)); }

// a TS cast in the callee position. `s_parenthesized` gets no site on purpose:
// measured 2026-09-04, babel does not emit ParenthesizedExpression under this
// parser configuration at all — `(f)(1)` is a plain identifier callee — so no
// corpus can produce that shape and it is waived rather than left `absent`.
export function useAs(n: number): number {
  return (curried as (m: number) => (k: number) => number)(n)(n);
}

// FOUR MORE OBJECT POSITIONS, and these are here rather than in alpha.mjs for
// a reason that is about the ORACLE. `(x as T).m()` and `x!.m()` cannot be
// spelt in a runnable .mjs at all. `(await p).m()` and `` `s`.m() `` CAN be,
// and they must not be: neither resolves today — the first waits on the
// control-form item and the second answers through the String prototype, which
// is the standard library — so a runnable site would show up as an edge the
// runtime takes and the model misses, which is UNSOUND. A shape whose residue
// is known and owned belongs in the corpus the oracle does not run.
// EVERY RECEIVER BELOW IS A REAL VALUE, and that is the whole care taken here.
// The first draft wrote `declare const held: Holder | null` and asked whether
// `held!.pick()` resolves — it does not, and the refusal would have been about
// an ambient declaration carrying no value rather than about the model. The
// same trap caught the `(cast as T)` probe an hour earlier and `maybe!()` in
// this very file a day earlier. A site measures the model only when everything
// except the construct under study already works.
const holder = { pick(n: number): number { return n; } };
type Holder = typeof holder;
async function mkHolder(): Promise<Holder> { return holder; }

// A computed callee whose key is a TEMPLATE with no expressions. The value is
// fixed at parse time, and until 2026-09-08 the scanner's four-relation
// contract could not carry it: TemplateElement.value is `{raw, cooked}`, a
// nested OBJECT, and only scalar own properties became ast_attr facts.
//
// THE CONTRACT MOVED and this site had to move with it. It used to read
// `` bag[`fixed`](n) ``, and `bag` is an AMBIENT DECLARATION carrying no value
// — so the call could not resolve however good the key was, and the site
// measured the receiver rather than the key. That is the trap this file's own
// header names, for the fourth time. `holder` is a real object with a real
// method, so what is under study here is the KEY and nothing else.
export function tmplKey(n: number): number { return holder[`pick`](n); }

export function onCast(n: number): number { return (holder as Holder).pick(n); }
export function onNonNull(n: number): number { return holder!.pick(n); }
// `mkHolder()` alone DOES reach `holder` through the return rule, so the only
// thing standing between this site and an edge is the `await` wrapper — which
// is `w_df_control_forms`, and this site is what will show it landing.
export async function onAwait(n: number): Promise<number> {
  return (await mkHolder()).pick(n);
}
// The receiver here is a String, not a value in this program: `concat` answers
// through the built-in prototype. Its residue is the standard library.
export function onTemplate(n: number): string { return `k${n}`.concat('!'); }

// A TAG THAT IS NOT A FUNCTION, and it is here rather than in a runnable file
// for the reason this file exists: `` stampObj`x` `` throws at runtime, so no
// executable fixture can hold it, and without it the `fn_node` guard on the
// tagged-template rule has nothing to bite on — the mutant that drops it
// derives a byte-identical world. `stampObj` is a REAL VALUE and not an ambient
// declaration, which is the care this file's header already demands: the site
// measures the guard only when everything except the guard already works.
const stampObj = { at: 1 };
// ...and NO `: unknown` return annotation, for the same reason the tag in
// alpha.mjs has no rest parameter: it would introduce `tsunknown_keyword`,
// which this vocabulary does not declare. The gate caught both on the first
// full run, which is the gate doing its job and the fixture doing too much.
export function onTagObject(n: number) { return stampObj`k${n}`; }

// AN ITERABLE WHOSE `next` IS NOT CALLABLE, and it is here for exactly the
// reason `stampObj` is. `for (const x of oneShot)` throws at run time — the
// protocol demands a callable `next` — so no executable fixture can hold it,
// and without a site the `fn_node` guard on the for-of's SECOND hop derives a
// byte-identical world when it is deleted. Measured 2026-09-07 before this was
// written: six mutants aimed at the iterator protocol, and that guard was one
// of the two survivors.
//
// THE VALUE IS AN OBJECT LITERAL AND NOT A NUMBER, which is the whole care.
// `{ next: 1 }` would have looked like the same site and measured nothing: a
// numeric literal is not in `node_value_kind`, so `may_be_node` never reaches
// it and the premise BEFORE the guard is what would have failed. The guard is
// only exercised when everything up to it succeeds.
const oneShot = { [Symbol.iterator]() { return { next: { at: 1 } }; } };
export function onIterObject(n: number): number {
  let s = 0;
  for (const x of oneShot) s += n;
  return s;
}

// A COMPUTED KEY THAT IS NOT A WELL-KNOWN SYMBOL, and the second survivor of
// that set. `key_name` in rules/js-structure.rofl reads a computed key through
// a `Symbol` guard, because `obj[Anything.else]` names a property this model
// cannot know — and the corpus contained exactly ONE computed key, the
// protocol's own, so dropping the guard changed no answer anywhere. It is not
// spellable in a runnable fixture for a duller reason than the others: it
// would run perfectly well, and a method the model must NOT name is a method
// the oracle would then see run under a name nobody derived.
const wellKnown = { spot: 'pick' };
export const aliasedKey = { [wellKnown.spot](n: number): number { return n; } };

// A DESTRUCTURED NAME AND A FREE ONE THAT LOOKS LIKE IT. The value arm for
// destructuring ends in `sees_binder`, and that guard had nothing to bite on in
// a runnable corpus: the fixture in alpha.mjs binds `taken` at module scope and
// uses it once, so a binder visible everywhere and a binder visible in its
// region are the same binder.
//
// HERE THEY ARE NOT. `inner` is bound INSIDE `scoped`, and `outside` calls a
// free identifier of the same name — which throws at run time, so no executable
// fixture can hold it. Without the scoping join the model would resolve
// `outside`'s call to the value bound in a function it is not in, and invent an
// edge. This is scope and NOT shadowing: nothing declares `inner` twice, so it
// asks nothing of w_scope_shadowing.
// `fetched` IS A PLAIN FUNCTION AND NOT `curried`, and the first draft used
// `curried`: `inner(n)(n)` is a call ON a call, so the free identifier left
// `s_call_result` — a shape every site of which resolved — carrying a residue
// with no reason, and `shape_unexplained[audit]` said so within one run. A site
// must introduce the construct it tests and NOTHING ELSE, and a second call was
// a second construct.
function fetched(n: number): number { return n; }
const cache = { fetchIt: fetched };

export function scoped(n: number): number {
  const { fetchIt: inner } = cache;
  return inner(n);
}

export function outside(n: number): number {
  return inner(n);
}

export async function dyn(p: string) { return import(p); }

// A REST BINDING AND THE KEY IT DID NOT TAKE. `const { bolted: usedBolted,
// ...leftovers } = fastenings` gives `leftovers` every key EXCEPT `bolted`, so
// `leftovers.riveted` is a function and `leftovers.bolted` is `undefined`.
//
// THE SECOND SITE IS WHY THIS IS HERE AND NOT IN alpha.mjs: calling
// `leftovers.bolted(n)` throws at run time, so no executable fixture can hold
// it — and it is the ONLY thing that can tell a rest rule that excludes the
// taken keys from one that copies them all. The exclusion is the whole content
// of the relation and it is unobservable on a runnable corpus.
function bolted(n: number): number { return n; }
function riveted(n: number): number { return n; }

const fastenings = { bolted, riveted };
const { bolted: usedBolted, ...leftovers } = fastenings;

export function pullsRest(n: number): number { return leftovers.riveted(n); }
export function pullsTaken(n: number): number { return usedBolted(n); }
export function pullsExcluded(n: number): number { return leftovers.bolted(n); }
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// LABELLED CONTROL, 2026-09-08 — queue item w_labelled_control, and the corpus
// contained ZERO labels before this block: `labeled_statement` 0 nodes,
// `break_statement` with a `label` child 0. So what the control-flow layer did
// with `break outer` was a GUESS, and the first thing this fixture bought was
// the measurement rather than the rule.
//
// SCANNED AND NOT RUN, and the reason is the oracle rather than the construct —
// every line here runs perfectly well. trace.mjs records CALL FRAMES, and what
// this fixture asks about is `after_abrupt`, which is not observable as a
// frame: a statement that never runs produces no evidence at all. A runnable
// copy would cost alpha.mjs's pinned counts and buy nothing.
//
// EACH POSITION IS A CALL TO A DISTINCTLY NAMED FUNCTION, which is the pattern
// `neverReached`/`neverCased` established in alpha.mjs: a statement has no name
// and a count of them measures the corpus, so the oracle joins `after_abrupt`
// through `resolves` and reads the CALLEE's name.
//
// EVERY LOOP HERE IS A `while` AND THE FIRST DRAFT USED `for...of`, which is the
// natural spelling and the wrong one. A `for...of` is a `transfer_kind` at the
// call graph, so ten of them walked into the iterator-protocol oracle in
// test/js-controlflow-values.test.ts — a named set of four loops, sorted by the
// function that holds them, whose whole point is which iterables the model can
// reach. `while` carries the same `guard_kind(_, body)` arm and asks nothing of
// the value layer, so the label work is measured without moving another item's
// instrument. A fixture is part of the corpus every other test reads.
function pastBreak(n: number): number { return n; }
function pastLabelledBreak(n: number): number { return n; }
function beyondLabel(n: number): number { return n; }

// `break outer` leaves the OUTER loop from inside the inner one — a transfer
// across a boundary no unlabelled `break` can cross. `pastBreak` is the
// ordinary arm (a sibling of the break in its own statement list, which
// `r_abrupt` already covered) and `pastLabelledBreak` is the one only a label
// can reach: it is a sibling of the INNER LOOP, one list further out.
// `beyondLabel` is the precision control — it sits after the labelled statement
// and it runs.
export function labelledBreak(n: number): number {
  let total = 0;
  outer: while (total < n) {
    while (total < n) {
      total = total + 1;
      break outer;
      pastBreak(n);
    }
    pastLabelledBreak(total);
  }
  return beyondLabel(total);
}

function pastContinue(n: number): number { return n; }
function pastLabelledContinue(n: number): number { return n; }

// ...and `continue outer` is the same walk with a different destination: the
// rest of the labelled loop's body is skipped for this iteration. The layer
// files break and continue under one mechanism and this fixture keeps them two
// sites, because one site would let an arm covering only `break` pass.
export function labelledContinue(n: number): number {
  let total = 0;
  rowLoop: while (total < n) {
    while (total < n) {
      total = total + 1;
      continue rowLoop;
      pastContinue(n);
    }
    pastLabelledContinue(total);
  }
  return total;
}

function pastBlockBreak(n: number): number { return n; }
function pastLabelledBlock(n: number): number { return n; }
function afterBlock(n: number): number { return n; }

// A LABEL ON A BLOCK, which is the form nothing but a label can produce: `blk`
// names no loop and no switch, so `break blk` is the only statement in the
// language that can leave it. A model that read a labelled break as an ordinary
// one would say the whole of this function's block runs — and that is not a
// hypothetical, it is what the model said before this item: a labelled block is
// not a loop body, not an `if` arm and not a switch case, so `pastLabelledBlock`
// was in NEITHER `guarded` NOR `may_not_run`.
export function labelledBlock(n: number): number {
  let total = 0;
  blk: {
    while (total < n) {
      total = total + 1;
      break blk;
      pastBlockBreak(n);
    }
    pastLabelledBlock(total);
  }
  return afterBlock(total);
}

function pastConditionalLabelledBreak(n: number): number { return n; }

// WHERE THIS ARM IS STRUCTURALLY UNABLE TO LOOK, put in the corpus as a ROW
// rather than left in a sentence. Every break above is UNCONDITIONAL in its own
// statement list, so reaching it is reaching it. Here the transfer sits under an
// `if`, which means `pastConditionalLabelledBreak` runs on every iteration whose
// test is false — and `after_abrupt`, whose own comment says NEVER, names it
// anyway, because the walk from the reference to the label crosses a guard arm
// without noticing. The `throwing_call` arm has had the same body shape since
// 2026-09-06 and was never given a site of its own.
export function conditionalLabelledBreak(n: number, off: number): number {
  let total = 0;
  cond: while (total < n) {
    while (total < n) {
      if (off > 0) break cond;
      total = total + 1;
    }
    pastConditionalLabelledBreak(total);
  }
  return total;
}

function pastPlainBreak(n: number): number { return n; }
function beyondPlainBreak(n: number): number { return n; }

// THE NEGATIVE CONTROL, and it is the whole content of the item. An UNLABELLED
// break leaves the inner loop and nothing else, so `beyondPlainBreak` runs on
// every iteration that reaches it. If the rule for the labelled form is written
// over `break_statement` rather than over the LABEL, this name appears beside
// `pastLabelledBreak` and the model has stopped telling the two apart.
//
// THE LABEL IS PRESENT AND UNREFERENCED ON PURPOSE. Without it this site only
// says "a function with no label behaves as before", which a rule that keyed on
// `break_statement` and happened to find no label would also satisfy. With it,
// the only thing standing between the plain `break` and `unused` is the `label`
// CHILD the reference does not have.
export function plainBreak(n: number): number {
  let total = 0;
  unused: while (total < n) {
    while (total < n) {
      total = total + 1;
      break;
      pastPlainBreak(n);
    }
    beyondPlainBreak(total);
  }
  return total;
}

function pastInnerBreak(n: number): number { return n; }
function pastInnerLabel(n: number): number { return n; }

// TWO LABELS, AND THE BREAK NAMES THE INNER ONE. Every other site here has one
// label per function, so "the label containing the reference" and "the label
// whose NAME the reference carries" are the same node and no site could tell a
// rule that joins on the name from one that does not. Here they differ:
// `break linner` leaves the inner loop only, so `pastInnerLabel` runs on every
// iteration, and a rule that took any enclosing label as the target would say it
// does not.
export function twoLabels(n: number): number {
  let total = 0;
  louter: while (total < n) {
    linner: while (total < n) {
      total = total + 1;
      break linner;
      pastInnerBreak(n);
    }
    pastInnerLabel(total);
  }
  return total;
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// THE INERT STATEMENTS, 2026-09-08 — queue item w_inert_statements, whose own
// note says "three statements no layer is likely to have an opinion about".
// LIKELY is a guess and this file exists so that verdicts are not written from
// guesses, so each position below is here to make one of the four layers say
// something rather than to make the count go up.
//
// `with` IS NOT HERE AND CANNOT BE. Measured 2026-09-08: scanners/js_ast.ts
// parses every file with `sourceType: 'module'`, modules are strict, and babel
// answers `'with' in strict mode. (1:0)` — a REFUSAL, not a node. The refusal
// is total: the scan returns `ast_parse_error` and ZERO ast_node facts, so a
// `with` anywhere in this file would delete the whole of it from the corpus.
// See w_inert_statements in facts/worklist.rofl for what the same source does
// under `sourceType: 'script'`, which is a different measurement with a
// different answer.
function seenEmpty(n: number): number { return n; }
function pastEmpty(n: number): number { return n; }

// FOUR POSITIONS FOR ONE STATEMENT WITH NO CHILDREN. `;` is a statement the
// scanner emits with ZERO `ast_child` rows, so there is nothing in it for a
// guard arm to skip and nothing after it inside itself — but it can OCCUPY a
// guarded position, and the two are different claims. Here it is a statement of
// its own, the body of a loop, an arm of an `if`, and a sibling after a
// `return` — which is where an inert statement could still change an answer,
// because `after_abrupt` counts INDEX and an empty statement consumes one.
export function inertEmpty(n: number): number {
  ;
  let total = n;
  while (total < 0) ;
  if (n < 0) ; else total = seenEmpty(total);
  return total;
  ;
  pastEmpty(total);
}

function pastDebugger(n: number): number { return n; }

// `debugger` is the one statement whose meaning is IMPLEMENTATION-DEFINED: the
// spec lets an implementation break here and requires nothing. It completes
// normally either way, which is why it is filed with the inert ones and not
// with the suspensions — a suspension is control leaving, and this is control
// stopping in place with the same continuation.
export function inertDebugger(n: number): number {
  debugger;
  const total = seenEmpty(n);
  return total;
  debugger;
  pastDebugger(total);
}
// THE TWO ERASURE MARKERS AN EXPORT CARRIES (w_export_specifier_forms,
// 2026-09-08), and this file is where they can be spelled at all: a `.mjs` has
// no `type` keyword, so the guards in `export_local` (rules/js-dataflow.rofl)
// had NO SITE in the runnable half of the corpus and their mutants would have
// survived for want of one rather than for want of a rule.
//
// NEITHER LINE DECLARES ANYTHING NEW. `Base` and `curried` are already here and
// already reached by the value layer, so with the guard in place these two rows
// derive NOTHING and with it removed they derive a name the module does not
// offer at runtime — which is exactly the difference the mutant measures. A
// fixture that also introduced a function would have moved the census for a
// question that is not about functions.
export type { Base as BaseType };
export { type curried as curriedType };

// DECORATORS AND ONE AUTO-ACCESSOR (w_plugin_gated_kinds, 2026-09-08). They are
// HERE and not in a `.mjs` for a reason that was measured rather than assumed:
// node 24.13 refuses both — `@log` is `SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token`
// and `accessor slot = 4` fails at the keyword — so no fixture of this shape can
// be reached by the execution oracle on this machine at all. That is a real
// limit on what the verdicts below can rest on, and it is stated in the ledger
// rather than left for a reader to discover.
//
// `@decoOnce` IS A CALL WITH NO CALL EXPRESSION. `@decoOnce class Decorated {}`
// evaluates `decoOnce` and calls it with the class and a context object at
// class-definition time, and the grammar shows no `call_expression` whatever —
// the same shape as a tagged template's tag and as `for-of`'s `Symbol.iterator`,
// both of which this layer already models, and the same shape as the accessor
// call it cannot yet model.
//
// `@decoFactory('m')` IS THE OTHER SHAPE and the pair is the point: the factory
// call IS in the grammar, and what is invisible is the call of its RESULT. One
// arm should reach both, because the value layer already carries what a call
// returns; whether it does is a measurement and not a hope.
// NO GENERICS AND NO `unknown` HERE, and that is not a style choice: the first
// draft wrote `decoOnce<T>(value: T, _ctx: unknown)` and `vocabulary_gap[audit]`
// immediately reported THREE kinds this item is not about —
// `tstype_parameter`, `tstype_parameter_declaration`, `tsunknown_keyword`. The
// second draft used `object` and added a fourth, `tsobject_keyword`. A fixture
// for one construct that quietly declares three others makes its own verdicts
// unattributable, so these two carry no annotation at all — `.ts` does not
// require one, and the only annotation left, `_name: string`, is a kind the
// vocabulary already declares.
function decoOnce(value, _ctx) { return value; }
function decoApplied(value, _ctx) { return value; }
function decoFactory(_name: string) { return decoApplied; }

@decoOnce
class Decorated {
  @decoFactory('m') marked(): number { return 1; }
  accessor slot = 4;
}
export { Decorated, decoOnce, decoApplied, decoFactory };
// =============================================================
// THREE VALUE FORMS THE VOCABULARY NEVER NAMED (w_update_and_literals,
// 2026-09-08): `i++`, `1n` and `/re/g`. Every position below exists to make
// one of the four layers say something, and each one was chosen AFTER the
// measurement that showed the layer said nothing.
//
// `seenUpdate` and `bumpedInUpdate` are the pair the control-flow half turns
// on, and the difference between them is the whole point: one is called from
// the BODY of a `for`, which `guard_kind(for_statement, body)` has always
// covered, and the other from its UPDATE, which had no row. Measured before
// the row was written, on the one C-style `for` this corpus already had
// (alpha.mjs:845): `guard_arm` named its body and NOT its `j += 1`, so the
// model positively asserted that a for-update runs — and `for (i = 0; i < 0;
// i++)` runs it zero times.
// ...and `readLimit` is the THIRD slot, which exists because a mutant needed
// it. `guard_kind(for_statement, test)` is a row somebody could plausibly add
// beside the right one, and it is FALSE — a `for`'s test runs at least once
// whenever its init completes. Measured without this function in the corpus,
// the mis-aimed row moved `guarded` from 385 to 394 and moved `may_not_run`
// and `guarded_call` NOT AT ALL, because no `for` in the corpus called
// anything in its test: a survivor for want of a site rather than for want of
// a rule. One call here turns it into a mutant that dies.
function seenUpdate(n: number): number { return n; }
function bumpedInUpdate(n: number): number { return n + 1; }
function readLimit(n: number): number { return n; }

export function updateForms(n: number): number {
  let i = 0;
  // POSTFIX AND PREFIX, both bound, because the two differ in the one place
  // this layer would have to look: `taken` is the value BEFORE the increment
  // and `given` the value after. Neither is carried, and the reason is
  // `plain_assign`'s reason for refusing `x += y` — the value is the result of
  // ToNumeric on the operand, so even a known literal operand does not give
  // this layer the answer: `"5"++` is the NUMBER 5.
  const taken = i++;
  const given = --i;
  let total = taken + given;
  for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) { total += seenUpdate(k); }
  for (let m = 0; m < n; m = bumpedInUpdate(m)) { total += m; }
  for (let p = 0; p < readLimit(n); p++) { total += p; }
  return total;
}

// A BIGINT'S VALUE REACHED THE STORE AS NOTHING AT ALL until the scanner
// learned the fourth scalar: `BigIntLiteral.value` is a native `bigint`, which
// matched none of the four branches in scanners/js_ast.ts, so `1n` was the one
// literal in JavaScript that arrived with no `ast_attr` row. `BIG_TOTAL` is
// bound so the value has to travel through `binder`, and `255n.toString(16)`
// is a member call ON a bigint literal — the residue that belongs to the
// standard library rather than to this program.
const BIG_TOTAL = 9007199254740993n;
export function bigForms(): string {
  return 255n.toString(16) + String(BIG_TOTAL);
}

// A REGEXP LITERAL IS THE ONLY LITERAL IN THIS LANGUAGE WHOSE VALUE IS AN
// OBJECT, which is why it is in `node_value_kind` beside `object_expression`
// and not in `literal_kind` beside `1n`. Two receivers on purpose: `MATCHER`
// reaches its prototype through the VALUE arm of `prototype_of` (binder ->
// may_be_node -> kind), and the inline `/x[0-9]/` reaches it through the KIND
// arm, so deleting either arm loses exactly one of them.
const MATCHER = /ab+c/gi;
//
// THE RETURN TYPE IS `number` AND THAT IS NOT A STYLE CHOICE: written
// `: boolean`, this line put `tsboolean_keyword` in the corpus and
// `vocabulary_gap[audit]` named it on the first run — a kind nobody had
// declared, arriving through a fixture written for a different question. The
// audit doing its job, and a reminder that a fixture's TYPES are corpus too.
export function regexpForms(s: string): number {
  return MATCHER.test(s) || /x[0-9]/.test(s) ? 1 : 0;
}
// ===========================================================================
// CLASS EXPRESSIONS, 2026-09-08 (w_class_expression), and the item's premise
// was that the model ALREADY had an opinion here — `obj_like[flow]` and
// `node_value_kind` both name `class_expression` — so the first job was to
// find out what that opinion DERIVES rather than to write a rule.
//
// MEASURED FIRST, on a probe carrying each form beside its control in one
// file. `new DeclaredClass().hold()` resolves; `new (class {})().hold()` and
// `new (class Inner {})().hold()` resolve to NOTHING, and both sites come back
// as unresolved `s_member_on_ident`. The cause is one relation: `class_named`
// reads a class's `id` CHILD, and a class expression either has no `id` at all
// or has one that is not the name it is used under — `const W = class Hoist {}`
// binds `W` on the outside and `Hoist` only inside its own body.
//
// The controls in that probe are load-bearing and are here too: a function
// expression and an arrow bound the same way behave identically at the modules
// layer, which is what says the `export const X = <expr>` silence is NOT a
// class-expression question.
// NO `: unknown` AND NO `as never` ANYWHERE BELOW, for the reason line 113 of
// this file already gives about the tag: a TS keyword kind nobody has governed
// lands in `kind_ungoverned[audit]` in the era layer. Measured, not foreseen —
// the first draft of this block carried both and test/js-env.test.ts named
// `tsnever_keyword` and `tsunknown_keyword` within one run.
const Crank = class { turn(n: number): number { return n; } };
// `Winch` CARRIES A CONSTRUCTOR so that the two naming rules can DISAGREE at a
// site. V8 names this frame `Hoist` — the class's own `id` — and names an
// anonymous one after its binding; without the negation in `anon_class` the
// model would derive both `Hoist` and `Winch` here and one of them is an edge
// no execution produces.
const Winch = class Hoist {
  constructor(n: number) { this.span = n; }
  lift(n: number): number { return n; }
  inner() { return Hoist; }
};
const Gantry = class {
  // NO DECLARED FIELD: `load: number` is a `class_property`, which is ES2022 and
  // is `w_class_fields`'s kind to put in this corpus, not this item's.
  constructor(n: number) { this.load = n; }
  static rated(n: number): number { return n; }
  bear(n: number): number { return n; }
};

export function onAnonClassExpr(n: number): number { return new Crank().turn(n); }
export function onNamedClassExpr(n: number): number { return new Winch(n).lift(n); }
// THE STATIC AND THE INSTANCE HALVES, which is why the fix belongs in
// `class_named` and not in the `new` rule alone: `class_receiver[flow]` decides
// which half of a class a receiver can see, and it reads the same relation.
// Without the class-expression arm `Gantry.rated(n)` reads the PROTOTYPE half
// and answers with an instance method, which is a TypeError at runtime.
export function onClassExprStatic(n: number): number { return Gantry.rated(n); }
export function onClassExprCtor(n: number): number { return new Gantry(n).bear(n); }
// ...and the heritage clause, which reaches the same relation a third way.
class Davit extends Crank { twice(n: number): number { return this.turn(n) + n; } }
export function onExtendsClassExpr(n: number): number { return new Davit().twice(n); }

// THE CONTROL-FLOW HALF, and it is the half that says a class expression is
// not inert. `class_declaration x controlflow` carries
// `a_no_control_transfer`, and for a HERITAGE CLAUSE that reason is false:
// `class extends mountOf() {}` calls `mountOf` when the class is EVALUATED,
// which for an expression is wherever the expression stands. Measured on a
// probe before this site existed — `calls_in` carried `top -> baseOf` for
// exactly this shape — and the same probe showed a computed method key
// (`[keyOf()]() {}`) attributed to the METHOD it keys rather than to the
// enclosing scope, which is w_computed_key_names' defect reached through a
// class expression rather than this item's.
function mountOf() { return Crank; }
export const Bracket = class extends mountOf() {
  fasten(n: number): number { return n; }
};

// META PROPERTY, 2026-09-08 (w_meta_property). ONE NODE KIND AND TWO
// CONSTRUCTS, and the scanner DOES tell them apart — measured, not assumed:
// every `meta_property` node carries NO `ast_attr` at all and two identifier
// children, `meta` and `property`, so `new.target` is (meta="new",
// property="target") and `import.meta` is (meta="import", property="meta").
//
// `import.meta.url` IS A READ AND NOT A CALL, deliberately. `import.meta`
// standing in a CALLEE-object position classifies as `o_other`, and
// facts/js-shapes.rofl waives that shape as `a_catch_all_empty_by_design`; a
// call here would make that waiver false for a reason that has nothing to do
// with this item. The residue is named in facts/worklist.rofl instead.
export function constructionMode(n: number) { return new.target ? n : null; }
export const moduleHere = import.meta.url;
// ===========================================================================
// ES2022 CLASS SYNTAX (w_class_fields, 2026-09-08). Five kinds the vocabulary
// named on 2026-09-08 for the denominator and no corpus site exercised:
// `class_property`, `class_private_property`, `class_private_method`,
// `private_name` and `static_block`.
//
// MEASURED BY RUNNING THE SHAPE BEFORE THE SITE WAS WRITTEN, and the timings
// are the whole reason the control-flow verdicts differ between two rows of the
// same class body:
//
//   at class DEFINITION      static mintMark = ...      static { ... }
//   at every `new`           face = ...    #edge = ...
//   never, if never `new`ed  face = ...    #edge = ...
//
// ...so a NON-STATIC field initialiser is an arm that may be skipped and a
// static one is not. See test/js-controlflow-values.test.ts, which runs it.
//
// V8 NAMES NEITHER FRAME AFTER A FUNCTION: a call inside a static block reports
// `<static_initializer>` and one inside an instance field reports
// `<instance_members_initializer>`, both with the class as the type name. That
// is why this fixture is in the SCANNED half — the execution oracle could not
// attribute these edges to a caller it has a name for.
function stamped(n: number): number { return n + 1; }
function minted(n: number): number { return n + 2; }
function sealed(n: number): number { return n + 3; }
function struck(n: number): number { return n + 4; }
function pressed(n: number): number { return n + 5; }
function notched(n: number): number { return n + 8; }
function burnished(n: number): number { return n + 9; }
function hammered(n: number): number { return n + 10; }

export class Coin {
  face = stamped(0);                          // class_property, instance
  #edge = minted(0);                          // class_private_property + private_name
  static mintMark = sealed(0);                // class_property, static
  static #tally = 0;                          // class_private_property, static
  static forge = (n: number) => hammered(n);  // a STATIC field whose value is one
  static pick = 'rim';                        // a field whose value is a LITERAL
  strike = (n: number) => struck(n);          // a field whose value is a function
  #mark = (n: number) => burnished(n);        // a PRIVATE field whose value is one
  blank;                                      // a field with NO initialiser

  // `this.strike(n)` here is the site for `class_method_of`: a PUBLIC member read
  // through `this` inside a PRIVATE method, which needs `this` to reach the class.
  #rim(n: number): number { return this.#edge + this.strike(n) + n; }
  get #face(): number { return pressed(0); }                // a PRIVATE ACCESSOR
  // A PUBLIC TWIN OF `#rim`, and it is the negative control the private
  // reading needs: `#rim` and `rim` are two different members of one class, so
  // a model that named a private member by the bare identifier under its
  // `private_name` would answer BOTH for `this.#rim(n)` and derive an edge to
  // `notched` that no execution takes.
  rim(n: number): number { return notched(n); }

  // `this` is the CLASS here, not an instance, and `Coin.#tally` is a private read
  // through a receiver that is not `this` at all — privacy is lexical either way.
  static { this.mintMark = Coin.#tally + 1; this.forge(0); }

  value(n: number): number {
    return this.face + this.#rim(n) + this.strike(n) + this.#mark(n) + (n > 0 ? this.#face : 0);
  }
}

export function usesCoin(n: number): number { return new Coin().value(n) + Coin.forge(n); }

// A SUBCLASS INHERITS ITS PARENT'S FIELDS AND A FIELD OF ITS OWN SHADOWS ONE,
// which is what makes `member_value` and `own_key` load-bearing for a field
// rather than merely true of one. MEASURED FIRST, and it is why these four lines
// exist: with the class-fields rules in and no subclass, deleting
// `member_value[flow](CD, Key, V) :- field_of[flow](CD, Key, _, V).` moved NOT
// ONE ROW - the receiver halves are derived from `field_of` directly - so the arm
// was decoration until something read it.
//
//   new Doubloon().strike(n)   an INSTANCE field declared only on Coin
//   Doubloon.forge(n)          a STATIC field declared only on Coin
//   Doubloon.pick              a static field the subclass SHADOWS, so the
//                              computed callee is `value` here and `rim` on Coin
function punched(n: number): number { return n + 11; }

export class Doubloon extends Coin {
  static pick = 'value';
  tint = punched(0);
}
export function usesDoubloon(n: number): number { return new Doubloon().strike(n) + Doubloon.forge(n); }
export function usesPicked(n: number): number { return new Coin()[Coin.pick](n); }
export function usesPickedSub(n: number): number { return new Doubloon()[Doubloon.pick](n); }

// A PRIVATE NAME IS LEXICAL, NOT A LOOKUP, and this is the site that says so.
// `new Inner().read()` returns Inner's `#tag` and not Outer's — measured by
// running the shape — so a rule that reached the private member through the
// receiver's VALUE would answer both here and be wrong about one of them.
function inked(n: number): number { return n + 6; }
function scored(n: number): number { return n + 7; }

export class Outer {
  #tag = inked(0);
  make(n: number): number {
    class Inner {
      #tag = scored(0);
      read(): number { return this.#tag; }
    }
    return new Inner().read() + this.#tag + n;
  }
}

// ...AND THE COLLISION THAT MAKES THE LEXICAL READING NECESSARY RATHER THAN
// TIDY: `"#edge"` is an ordinary string key and a legal one, measured. A model
// that spelled the private name `#edge` in the same key namespace would answer
// this object for a read of `this.#edge` and the class for a read of
// `plated["#edge"]`.
const plated = { '#edge': 'a string key, not a private name' };
export function reachesPlated(): string { return plated['#edge']; }

// TWO LIBRARY METHODS WITH TWO DIFFERENT YEARS (w_env_api_surface, 2026-09-08),
// and the pair is the point rather than either one. `bigint.toString` was
// already here and is ES2020; `at` is declared in lib.es2022.array.d.ts and
// `replaceAll` in lib.es2021.string.d.ts, so the three of them are unsupported
// under three DIFFERENT sets of environments. A single site would have shown a
// gate that fires; three sites a year apart show a gate that DISCRIMINATES,
// which is the claim `lib_unsupported[audit]` actually makes.
//
// NEITHER METHOD IS A NODE IN THIS PROGRAM, which is what puts them in
// `stdlib_member[audit]`'s residue in the first place — the receiver's kind is
// the whole of what the model knows, and the library says the rest.
// AND THE LIMIT, IN THE SAME FIXTURE AND MEASURED RATHER THAN DESCRIBED. The
// surface reaches a receiver whose PROTOTYPE the value layer knows, and it knows
// one from the receiver's KIND. `'aaa'.replaceAll(...)` is a string literal and
// is attributed; `s.replaceAll(...)` — the same method on a PARAMETER annotated
// `string` — is not, because a TypeScript annotation is not a value the model
// carries. Both lines are here so the gap is a row rather than a sentence.
export function libEras(s: string): string {
  const picked = [1, 2, 3].at(0);
  const known = 'aaa'.replaceAll('a', 'b');
  return known + s.replaceAll('a', 'b') + String(picked);
}

// A DIRECTIVE IS NOT AN EXPRESSION STATEMENT (w_directives, 2026-09-08), and
// this is the FUNCTION-BODY half of the fixture — delta.mjs carries the
// program-level one and the hashbang, because both of those have to be at the
// top of a file. babel puts a directive prologue in a `directives` ARRAY on the
// body and NOT in `body`, so every rule in this model that walks statements is
// structurally unable to see one.
//
// THE SECOND STRING IS A DIRECTIVE TOO. A directive prologue is any run of
// string-literal statements at the head of a body; `'use strict'` is only the
// one the language assigns a meaning to, and `'use rofl'` is the control that
// says the model must not be reading the TEXT. Both are `directive_literal`
// nodes carrying an `ast_value`, and nothing in the model reads either.
export function strictBody(n: number): number {
  'use strict';
  'use rofl';
  return n + 1;
}
// =============================================================
// A DECORATOR RETURNS A REPLACEMENT (w_decorator_replaces_its_target, 62).
// The CALL a decorator makes landed on 2026-09-08 as `r_decorator_call`; what
// it does to the thing it decorates did not. `@decoFerrule class Swage {}`
// binds `Swage` to whatever `decoFerrule` gave back, and until this block the
// value layer answered the ORIGINAL class for every read of that name.
//
// THE TWO DECORATORS ALREADY IN THIS FILE COULD NOT SHOW IT, and that is why
// these are here rather than a rule being written against them: `decoOnce` and
// `decoApplied` both `return value`, a PARAMETER, and a decorator call has no
// argument nodes in the grammar at all — so `may_be_node` of both decorator
// nodes was measured EMPTY, and a replacement rule over them would have derived
// nothing while looking finished. A decorator that returns a NAMED thing is the
// smallest site at which the question has an answer to be right or wrong about.
//
// `Swage.spliced(n)` IS THE OBSERVATION, and it is chosen so that the original
// cannot answer it: `Swage` declares no members whatever, so the edge exists
// only if the name reaches `Ferrule`. The alternative — giving both classes the
// same method — would have derived the same edge NAME either way and measured
// nothing.
function swaged(n: number): number { return n + 31; }
function crimped(n: number): number { return n + 32; }
function slung(n: number): number { return n + 33; }
function bitted(n: number): number { return n + 34; }

class Ferrule {
  static spliced(n: number): number { return swaged(n); }
}
function decoFerrule(_value, _ctx) { return Ferrule; }
function decoCrimp(_value, _ctx) { return crimped; }
function decoBitt(_value, _ctx) { return bitted; }

@decoFerrule
class Swage {}
export function usesSwage(n: number): number { return Swage.spliced(n); }

// A DECORATED METHOD AND AN AUTO-ACCESSOR IN ONE CLASS. `seized` is replaced by
// `crimped` — a method decorator returns the new method — and `sling` is an
// auto-accessor whose value is a function, which is the shape that gives
// `class_accessor_property` anything to say at either layer: the corpus had a
// DECLARATION and no READ, so both its cells were open for want of a site
// rather than for want of a rule.
// THE STATIC ONE IS NOT DECORATION EITHER. `class_member_static` and
// `class_member_proto` read the flag off the DECORATED MEMBER and not off what
// came back — a replacement is an ordinary function and carries no `static`
// attribute — so without a decorated static method the static half of that pair
// has no site and its mutant cannot die. `decoBitt` is a THIRD decorator rather
// than a reuse of `decoCrimp` for the same reason the two classes above have
// different members: one replacement reached through two arms would derive the
// same edge either way and measure neither.
//
// `#tucked` AND `tucked` ARE THE NEGATIVE CONTROL, on the pattern `#rim`/`rim`
// already sets in this file. `decorated_member` restricts itself to
// `class_method`, and `class_method_of` carries a PRIVATE method too — so
// without that one literal a decorated private method would enter
// `member_value` under its bare name and `new Thimble().tucked(n)` would answer
// the replacement of a member it cannot see. A private name is lexical and
// never reaches a receiver lookup; these two lines are what makes that
// statement falsifiable instead of true by absence.
class Thimble {
  @decoCrimp seized(n: number): number { return slung(n); }
  @decoBitt static tightened(n: number): number { return slung(n); }
  @decoCrimp #tucked(n: number): number { return slung(n); }
  accessor sling = slung;
  tucked(n: number): number { return bitted(n) + this.#tucked(n); }
  hauls(n: number): number { return this.sling(n); }
}
export function usesThimble(n: number): number {
  return new Thimble().seized(n) + new Thimble().hauls(n) + Thimble.tightened(n);
}
export function usesTucked(n: number): number { return new Thimble().tucked(n); }

// TWO DEPRECATED LIBRARY CALLS (w_env_api_surface, 2026-09-08), and the pair is
// the point: `substr` is deprecated and names NO replacement, `trimLeft` is
// deprecated and names `trimStart`. Measured over the ecmascript lib files —
// forty-one deprecations, two of which name a replacement — so a site for each
// half is a site for the whole relation, and `lib_call_remedy[audit]` having
// exactly one row is a fact about the SOURCE rather than about this fixture.
export function legacyString(s: string): string {
  return 'abc'.substr(0, 1) + 'abc'.trimLeft() + s;
}

// ===========================================================================
// THE CALLER, WHEN THE LANGUAGE PERFORMS THE CALL, 2026-09-08
// (w_meta_property + w_await_is_a_call_the_oracle_places_elsewhere).
//
// TWO SITES, ONE QUESTION, AND BOTH ARE HERE RATHER THAN IN A RUNNABLE FILE
// FOR THE SAME MEASURED REASON: the execution oracle CANNOT SEE EITHER OF THEM.
// `runOracle` in test/js-callgraph.test.ts keeps a frame only when the CALLER's
// file is a run file, and trace.mjs writes `file: st[1] ? ... : ''` — so an
// edge with no caller frame carries `""` and is dropped. Measured on a live
// probe: a thenable's `.then` reports `<top> -> settle  file="" line=0`, and it
// does not survive the filter. A site in alpha.mjs would therefore be judged by
// an instrument structurally unable to look at it.
//
// ---- 1. AN AWAIT REALLY DOES CALL SOMETHING, AND IT IS NOT WHAT THE QUEUE
// SAID. w_await_is_a_call recorded the callee as `Promise.prototype.then`, a
// standard-library method with no node. MEASURED and false: with
// `Promise.prototype.then` monkey-patched and a positive control that the patch
// is live (`p.then(f)` counts 1), `await <native promise>` calls it ZERO times
// on V8 11.3 (node 20.20.0) and V8 13.6 (node 24.13.0) - the versions are
// `process.versions.v8` and not the pair this repository has been quoting; see
// f_the_v8_version_pair_this_repository_quotes_is_not_the_one_it_runs. The
// spec's Await uses
// PerformPromiseThen, an INTERNAL operation — there is no observable call at
// all. What DOES get called is a user thenable's OWN `then`, exactly once.
//
// So the corpus's four existing awaits perform NO CALL (their arguments are all
// native promises, and `member_value[flow](_, "then", _)` is 0 of 162 keys),
// and this is the one shape where an await has a callee this program contains.
//
// AND THE CALLER IS NOBODY. The same probe reports the frame as a stack of
// DEPTH ONE — `st[1]` is undefined — so `settleThen` runs with no caller frame
// whatsoever. `<top>` in trace.mjs is what that ABSENCE renders as, and it is
// the same string that file writes for a call from module top level, which is a
// real region with real code. The model must not draw `awaitsThenable ->
// settleThen`: `performed_call[code]` says the call happens and refuses to name
// a caller, which is what this layer means by a caller when the language calls.
function settleThen(res: (v: number) => number) { res(1); }
const userThenable = { then: settleThen };
export async function awaitsThenable(n: number): Promise<number> {
  await userThenable;
  return n;
}

// ---- 2. `import.meta.resolve(...)` IS A CALL INTO THE HOST, and the note that
// kept it out of the corpus is discharged rather than ignored. It said a call
// here would land in `s_member_on_other`, whose waiver
// `a_catch_all_empty_by_design` would then be false for another item's reason.
// `obj_kind_class(meta_property, o_meta)` gives the receiver a name of its own,
// so the catch-all stays empty and this site is classified rather than swept.
//
// THE CALLEE IS THE HOST'S AND NOT THE LANGUAGE'S, and TypeScript's own files
// say so: `interface ImportMeta` in `lib.es5.d.ts` is EMPTY — `url` and
// `resolve` are declared in `lib.dom.d.ts` and in `@types/node`. `releaseOf` in
// scanners/ts_lib.ts returns null for both, by construction, because neither
// file name carries a release. So the standard-library surface that answered
// `array.join` is structurally unable to answer this one, and the residue is
// `no_source_target` rather than a queue entry.
export function resolvesHere(spec: string): string {
  return import.meta.resolve(spec);
}

// ===========================================================================
// A COMPUTED KEY THAT IS A BARE IDENTIFIER (w_computed_key_names, 2026-09-09),
// and it is the site the item said had to exist before the fix could be
// measured rather than argued.
//
// THE DEFECT. `key_name`'s first arm was `key_name(K, N) :- ast_name(K, N)`,
// unguarded and in ANY position, so for `{ [haspSpelling]() {} }` — where the
// key node IS the identifier — the model named the property `haspSpelling`.
// That is the name of the VARIABLE. The property is really called `latch`, and
// nothing in this program says so statically: the key is whatever the variable
// held when the object was evaluated. The `Symbol` guard three lines below the
// arm says exactly this must not happen, and it sits on the OTHER arm — the one
// that reads a computed key written as a MEMBER expression, which
// `[haspSpelling]` is not. `aliasedKey` above is the member form of the same
// shape; this is the bare-identifier form the guard could not look at.
//
// IT IS HERE AND NOT IN A RUNNABLE FIXTURE, and that is the item's own reason
// rather than convenience: a method the model must NOT name is a method the
// execution oracle would see run under a name nobody derived. `jamb.latch(1)`
// runs; `jamb.haspSpelling` is `undefined`. So the shape belongs where the
// CLASSIFIER is measured against the grammar and the oracle is not consulted,
// which is what this file's header says it is for.
//
// NOTHING CALLS THEM, DELIBERATELY. Adding a call would move `calls_in` and
// `resolves` in the same diff as the naming change, and then no reader could
// attribute either. What this site needs to be read by is `key_name`,
// `member_value`, `obj_member_fn`, `own_key` and `fn_name`, and every one of
// those derives over a declaration.
//
// THE SPELLING `haspSpelling` IS THE ORACLE'S HANDLE. It occurs nowhere else in
// the corpus, so `no relation in this model names anything haspSpelling` is an
// assertion no other branch's fixture can move.
const haspSpelling = 'latch';
export const jamb = {
  [haspSpelling](n: number): number { return n; },
  staple(n: number): number { return n; },
};
export class Clasp {
  [haspSpelling](n: number): number { return n; }
  hinge(n: number): number { return n; }
}
// ...AND THE PROPERTY FORM BESIDE THE METHOD FORM, because they are different
// rules and only one of them was reached by the method site. `{ [k]() {} }` is
// an `object_method`; `{ [k]: () => {} }` is an `object_property` whose value
// is a function, and `fn_name`, `member_value` and `obj_member_fn` each have a
// SEPARATE arm for it. Measured 2026-09-09: with only the method form here,
// three of the six arms that name a key were never asked the question.
export const sill = {
  [haspSpelling]: (n: number): number => n,
  bolt: (n: number): number => n,
};
// ...AND THE PATTERN FORM, which discharges a mutant that has been sitting in
// test/js-controlflow-values.test.ts marked WAITING ON AN ITEM. That comment
// says reading `ast_name` on a pattern's key where `destructures` reads
// `key_name` derives a byte-identical world, because every key in a pattern in
// this corpus is a plain identifier — and that it would bite on
// `const { [k]: v } = o`, which could not be written honestly until this item
// settled what a computed key is NAMED. It is settled: nothing.
//
// AND THE ANSWER HAS A PRICE THAT IS WORTH SEEING. `destructures` links a LOCAL
// to a KEY, so a pattern with no derivable key binds no local: `pried` is a
// name this program certainly binds and the model attributes to nothing, and
// the declarator is therefore not a `scoped_binder` either. That is the honest
// under-approximation — the key really is unknowable here — and it is the
// opposite failure from the one this item removed, which invented a key.
//
// NOTHING USES `pried`, deliberately: a call on it would be an unresolved call
// site, which moves the shape census for a reason that has nothing to do with
